hmmt-feb-2010-alg-01.title: Square and combine
hmmt-feb-2010-alg-01.body:
Squaring $x-y^2=3$ gives $x^2+y^4-2xy^2=9$. Subtract this from twice the second equation: $x^2+2xy^2+y^4=17$, i.e. $(x+y^2)^2=17$. Since $x,y>0$, $x+y^2=\sqrt{17}$.

Adding $x-y^2=3$: $2x=3+\sqrt{17}$, so $x=\frac{3+\sqrt{17}}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{3+\sqrt{17}}{2}$**

hmmt-feb-2010-alg-02.title: Build greedily
hmmt-feb-2010-alg-02.body:
If $A,B<\frac14$ have rank 3 and $b_1<a_1$, then $A<\frac1{a_1-1}\le\frac1{b_1}<B$. So the largest such number has the smallest possible $a_1$, and then (same argument one level down) the smallest possible $a_2$, and so on: build $q$ greedily by repeatedly adding the largest unit fraction that keeps the sum below $\frac14$.

- $\frac15$ is the largest unit fraction below $\frac14$, so $a_1=5$.
- $\frac14-\frac15=\frac1{20}$, and the largest unit fraction below it is $\frac1{21}$, so $a_2=21$.
- $\frac1{20}-\frac1{21}=\frac1{420}$, and the largest unit fraction below it is $\frac1{421}$, so $a_3=421$.

**Answer: $(5,21,421)$**

hmmt-feb-2010-alg-03.title: Track the sequence after a zero
hmmt-feb-2010-alg-03.body:
Suppose $S_N=0$. Then $a_{N+1}=1$ since $S_N<N+1$, so $S_{N+1}=N+1$. Then $a_{N+2}=1$ (as $N+1<N+2$), $S_{N+2}=2N+3$; then $a_{N+3}=-1$ and $S_{N+3}=N$; $a_{N+4}=1$, $S_{N+4}=2N+4$; $a_{N+5}=-1$, $S_{N+5}=N-1$; and so on. Inductively, for $i\ge1$,
$$S_{N+2i}=2N+2+i,\qquad S_{N+1+2i}=N+1-i.$$
The odd-offset values decrease to $0$ first when $i=N+1$, i.e. at $k=N+1+2(N+1)=3N+3$. So consecutive zeros satisfy $p_{n+1}=3p_n+3$.

The zeros are $0,3,12,39,120,363,1092,3279,\dots$ The largest not exceeding $2010$ is $1092$.

**Answer: 1092**

hmmt-feb-2010-alg-04.title: Eliminate
hmmt-feb-2010-alg-04.body:
Multiply the first equation by $k$ and subtract the second: $ak^4-a=0$. Since $a\ne0$, $k^4=1$, so $k\in\{1,-1,i,-i\}$.

All occur: with $a=b=c=d=1$, the numbers $-1,i,-i$ are roots of both polynomials (both equal $x^3+x^2+x+1$ up to order). With $a=b=c=1$, $d=-3$: both polynomials vanish at $x=1$ ($1+1+1-3=0$ in each).

**Answer: $1,-1,i,-i$**

hmmt-feb-2010-alg-05.title: Reduce to a polynomial in $b=x^2+y^2$
hmmt-feb-2010-alg-05.body:
Let $b=x^2+y^2$ and $a=2xy$, so $a+b=(x+y)^2=1$ and $(x-y)^2=b-a=2b-1$. Hence $x,y=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{2b-1}}2$ and, with $s=\sqrt{2b-1}$,
$$x^{20}+y^{20}=\frac{(1+s)^{20}+(1-s)^{20}}{2^{20}}=\frac{2}{2^{20}}\left[s^{20}+\binom{20}2s^{18}+\binom{20}4s^{16}+\cdots\right],$$
and $s^2=2b-1$, so this is a polynomial of degree 10 in $b$:
$$\frac{2}{2^{20}}\left[(2b-1)^{10}+\tbinom{20}{2}(2b-1)^9+\cdots\right]=20.$$

The polynomial $p(x)=x^{20}+(1-x)^{20}-20$ has no repeated roots (a common root of $p$ and $p'$ would be a common root of $x^{19}-20$ and $(1-x)^{19}-20$, i.e. $x=\sqrt[19]{20}\,\omega^m$ and $1-x=\sqrt[19]{20}\,\omega^n$ with $\omega=e^{2\pi i/19}$; comparing imaginary parts forces $m=n$, and then $x=1-x$ gives $x=\frac12$, so $20=2^{-19}$, a contradiction). Each $b$ corresponds to one unordered pair $\{x,y\}$, so the degree-10 polynomial in $b$ has 10 distinct roots, and we want their sum.

By Vieta, the sum is $-[b^9]/[b^{10}]$. Up to the common factor $\frac{2}{2^{20}}$: $[b^{10}]=2^{10}$ and $[b^9]=-10\cdot2^9+\binom{20}2 2^9$. Thus
$$-\frac{[b^9]}{[b^{10}]}=\frac{10\cdot2^9-190\cdot2^9}{2^{10}}=\frac{-180}{2}=-90.$$

**Answer: $-90$**

hmmt-feb-2010-alg-06.title: Upper bound and construction
hmmt-feb-2010-alg-06.body:
If $p$ had more than $1005$ minus signs, then $p(1)=1+(\text{2010 signs})<0$ (the sum of $2011$ terms $\pm1$ with at least $1006$ negative is negative). But $p(2)\ge2^{2010}-2^{2009}-\cdots-2-1=1>0$. By the Intermediate Value Theorem $p$ has a root in $(1,2)$. So at most $1005$ minus signs.

Construction: $p(x)=\frac{x^{2011}+1}{x+1}=x^{2010}-x^{2009}+x^{2008}-\cdots-x+1$ has exactly $1005$ minus signs. The only real root of $x^{2011}+1$ is $-1$, but $p(-1)=2011\ne0$, so $p$ has no real roots.

**Answer: 1005**

hmmt-feb-2010-alg-07.title: Express $\frac1{x-1}$ etc.
hmmt-feb-2010-alg-07.body:
From $a=\frac{b+c}{x-2}$ get $x-1=\frac{a+b+c}{a}$, so $\frac1{x-1}=\frac{a}{a+b+c}$ (note $a+b+c\neq0$, otherwise $x-1=0$ and the equations degenerate). Similarly $\frac1{y-1}=\frac b{a+b+c}$, $\frac1{z-1}=\frac c{a+b+c}$. Adding,
$$\frac1{x-1}+\frac1{y-1}+\frac1{z-1}=1.$$
Clearing denominators: $\sum(y-1)(z-1)=\prod(x-1)$, i.e.
$$(xy+yz+zx)-2(x+y+z)+3=xyz-(xy+yz+zx)+(x+y+z)-1.$$
So $xyz=2(xy+yz+zx)-3(x+y+z)+4=134-6030+4=-5892$.

**Answer: $-5892$**

hmmt-feb-2010-alg-08.title: Interpolation and finite differences
hmmt-feb-2010-alg-08.body:
For each permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,\dots,6\}$, Lagrange interpolation gives exactly one polynomial of degree at most $5$ with $p(k)=\sigma(k)$ (two such would differ by a nonzero polynomial of degree $\le5$ with $6$ roots). So there are $6!=720$ candidates, and we must remove those of degree less than $5$.

The degree is less than $5$ iff the fifth finite difference vanishes: $p(1)-5p(2)+10p(3)-10p(4)+5p(5)-p(6)=0$. Mod $5$ this gives $p(1)\equiv p(6)$, so $\{p(1),p(6)\}=\{1,6\}$. By symmetry ($p\mapsto7-p$) take $p(1)=1,p(6)=6$ and double. The equation becomes $-p(2)+2p(3)-2p(4)+p(5)=1$ with $\{p(2),\dots,p(5)\}=\{2,3,4,5\}$. Mod $2$, $p(2),p(5)$ have opposite parity; checking the cases leaves exactly three solutions $(p(2),p(3),p(4),p(5))=(2,3,4,5),(3,4,5,2),(5,3,2,4)$. So $2\cdot3=6$ permutations give lower degree, and the answer is $720-6=714$.

**Answer: 714**

hmmt-feb-2010-alg-08.title: Computer-style check
hmmt-feb-2010-alg-08.body:
Equivalently, the leading coefficient is $\frac1{120}\left(v_1-5v_2+10v_3-10v_4+5v_5-v_6\right)$ for the value list $v=(p(1),\dots,p(6))$; enumerating all $720$ permutations, exactly $6$ make this zero, leaving $714$.

**Answer: 714**

hmmt-feb-2010-alg-09.title: Track the largest preimage
hmmt-feb-2010-alg-09.body:
Roots of $f^n$ are preimages of $0$ under $f^n$. Preimages of $r$ under $f$ are the two roots of $cx^2-cx-r=0$, summing to $1$; they are real iff $r\ge-\frac c4$. So all roots of every $f^n$ are real iff all of them stay $\ge-\frac c4$; by the pairing symmetry $r\leftrightarrow1-r$ this is equivalent to all roots being $\le1+\frac c4$.

Let $g(x)=\frac12\left(1+\sqrt{1+\frac{4x}c}\right)$ be the larger inverse of $f$. The largest root of $f^n$ is $g^n(0)$, which increases to the fixed point $x_0=1+\frac1c$ (solving $cx(x-1)=x$). So we need $1+\frac1c\le1+\frac c4$, i.e. $c\ge2$.

For $c=2$: $x_0=\frac32=1+\frac c4$, and $g^n(0)<x_0$ for all $n$, so all roots lie in $[-\frac12,\frac32]$ and are real.

**Answer: 2**

hmmt-feb-2010-alg-10.title: Conjugate a commuting pair
hmmt-feb-2010-alg-10.body:
The cubics $f(x)=ax^3$ and $g(x)=-ax^3$ commute under composition. If $h(x)=x+b$, then $h^{-1}fh$ and $h^{-1}gh$ also commute (associativity of composition) and are cubic. Take $p=h^{-1}fh=a(x+b)^3-b$ and $q=h^{-1}gh=-a(x+b)^3-b$. The conditions $p(0)=-24,q(0)=30$ read $ab^3-b=-24$ and $-ab^3-b=30$, so $b=-3$, $a=1$.

Thus $p(x)=(x-3)^3+3$, $q(x)=-(x-3)^3+3$, giving $p(3)=3$ and $q(6)=-27+3=-24$.

The whole family $p=tx(x-3)(x-6)+9x-24$, $q=-tx(x-3)(x-6)-9x+30$ commutes, and $p(3)=3$, $q(6)=-24$ for every $t$, so the pair is determined.

**Answer: $(3,-24)$**
